checkpoints: BM25 scores are unbounded and corpus-dependent — they shift with term rarity, document length, and index size — while cosine similarity is naturally bounded to [-1, 1], so the two lists don't measure the same kind of quantity to begin with.

Min-max normalizing each list separately to [0, 1] only rescales each list onto the same axis labels; it doesn't make the underlying quantities comparable, so summing the two normalized values produces a number with no real relevance meaning.

A single outlier score in one engine's list — one document scoring far above the rest — stretches that list's min-max range and squashes every other document's normalized value toward zero, letting the outlier dominate the fused sum almost regardless of what the other engine reports.

Because min-max normalization is relative to whatever scores happen to be in the current result set, a shift in one engine's score distribution — reindexing, a corpus change, a scoring tweak — changes a document's normalized value and therefore the fused ranking, even though the document's actual rank and relevance haven't moved at all.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion sidesteps both failures by fusing on each engine's integer rank rather than its raw score, summing 1/(k+rank) with k = 60 — rank is always comparable across engines no matter what a raw score means or how its distribution shifts, so there's no normalization step left to be fragile.

A constructive code review affirms that combining both engines' signal into one ranking is the right goal, and frames rank-based fusion as the standard, battle-tested way to reach that goal rather than treating the author's intent as wrong.

Regression tests for a score-fusion function should specifically cover an outlier-score scenario and a distribution-shift scenario, asserting that a rank-based fusion keeps the ranking stable in both cases where the min-max version would visibly break.
